turns.t: Mr Whitlock, good to see you. I have the letter your daughter dropped in last week, and it mentions a couple of tumbles.
Oh, Susan fusses. It's two falls, that's all, and one of them was only because the cat was under my feet.
Tell me about the unsteadiness itself. When did you first notice it?
About six weeks ago I started feeling unsteady on my feet, like standing on a boat deck. My late wife always said I walked like a sailor anyway.
Ha. And the falls, when did they happen?
Both this month. The first in the kitchen, the second getting out of the armchair. Bang, down I went, right in front of the telly.
Getting out of the armchair, interesting. We'll come back to that. Let's go through your tablets, since you've brought the list.
I brought the lot. Susan wrote it out in her best handwriting. She's ever so proud of her handwriting.
Lovely. Start at the top. What's the first one?
Ramipril, 10 mg once a day, and that's for my high blood pressure.
Good. And the next one?
Tamsulosin, 400 micrograms once a day, for my enlarged prostate. I always call it the plumbing tablet, though.
Ha, the plumbing tablet. Any more?
Simvastatin, 40 mg, which I take at night. And aspirin, 75 mg, one a day.
And is that everything?
There's the stomach one, lansoprazole, 15 mg every morning. That's the five of them altogether.
Five. Do you take the ramipril and the tamsulosin at the same time of day?
Both first thing with my tea. My friend Ron takes his in the evening, and he's got a whole theory about it.
Ron's theory can wait. Let's check your pressure properly, sitting first.
Sitting, it's 128 over 74 and your pulse is 66. Now stand up for me, nice and slowly.
Standing, 104 over 62. Oxygen is 97 percent, and temperature 36.5 degrees Celsius.
Is that good? I never know what the numbers mean. My wife used to keep all that in a little book.
The standing one is lower than I'd like. That fits with what you told me about getting out of the chair.
Oh, so it's my blood pressure? Funny, because it was high when they first put me on the tablets.
I think the tablets are probably dropping your pressure too much when you stand, which would make anyone wobbly.
But I've taken them for years!
Bodies change as we get older. What suited you at seventy can be too much at seventy-eight.
I won't change anything today. I'd like some blood tests first, to check your kidneys and your blood count.
Blood again? They've taken so much I'll end up a prune.
Just the one tube this time. And I'd like a heart tracing, an ECG, while you're here.
Right now? I haven't even finished my tea.
It takes a few minutes. First, a bit of history. Have you had any operations?
A cataract operation, two years ago. Lovely job, I could suddenly see the telly clearer than the plot.
Ha. And in the family, anyone with brittle bones?
My mother had osteoporosis. Bent right over by the end, poor soul.
Thank you. Until the results are back, sit for a count of ten before you stand, and hold on to something solid.
Count to ten. I'll tell Ron about that one, he'll love it.
Please do. I'd like to see you again in two weeks, with the results.
Two weeks. Susan will drive me, bless her.
Perfect. Pop along to the nurse for the ECG, and mind the step on your way.
